intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that infantile-onset neurodegeneration with optic atrophy and structural brain abnormalities-2 (NDOABA2) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the BORCS5 gene.

checks.claim: Infantile-onset neurodegeneration with optic atrophy and structural brain abnormalities-2 (NDOABA2) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the BORCS5 gene.
checks.evidence_quote: Trio exome sequencing identified a homozygous c.283 C>T; p.(Arg95Ter) variant in exon 3 of the BORCS5 gene (NM_058169.4) in each of the couple's fetuses
checks.explanation: The paper links a homozygous BORCS5 variant to neuroaxonal dystrophy with osteopetrosis (OMIM 600329). It does not use the name NDOABA2 or mention compound heterozygous mutations.

paragraphs.text: Infantile-onset neurodegeneration with optic atrophy and structural brain abnormalities-2 (NDOABA2) is an autosomal recessive neurologic disorder with a broad phenotypic spectrum. Individuals with biallelic missense or splice-site variants have a developmental and epileptic encephalopathy. Features include profound intellectual disability, seizures beginning in the first year of life, optic neuropathy, progressive spasticity, and progressive movement disorders. Brain imaging shows hypomyelination, abnormalities of the corpus callosum, and progressive global cerebral atrophy. Homozygous protein-truncating variants cause a prenatally lethal phenotype with arthrogryposis multiplex congenita, brain malformations, and neuropathologic evidence of neuroaxonal dystrophy (Mencacci et al., 2026).

paragraphs.text: Mencacci et al. (2026) reported 16 affected individuals from 9 unrelated families of Pakistani, Moroccan, and Arab descent, 2 of the Arab families being from Oman. Ten individuals from 6 families shared a core phenotype of developmental encephalopathy with profound intellectual disability, delayed milestones, seizures, and progressive movement disorders with spasticity. None of these individuals achieved speech or walking, and all were completely dependent on others. Patients in 4 of the families had developmental regression, including loss of babbling, visual tracking, head control, and the ability to stand. Seizures began within the first year of life in all patients. In 3 families the seizures were controlled with standard antiepileptic treatment, and the older individuals in 1 family became seizure-free in their teens. Affected individuals from 2 other families had more severe epilepsy, with treatment-resistant infantile spasms, myoclonic seizures, and hypsarrhythmia on EEG.

paragraphs.text: All 10 individuals had progressive spasticity, diffuse hyperreflexia, bilateral extensor plantar responses, and severe limb contractures. Dystonia and parkinsonism were prominent in 2 families. Generalized dystonia led to scoliosis, painful spasms, and oculogyric crises, and the parkinsonian features included severe limb bradykinesia and hypomimia. Dystonic spasms improved dramatically with carbidopa/levodopa. Trihexyphenidyl, baclofen, and diazepam helped manage spasticity and dystonia. All patients had optic neuropathy. Nerve conduction studies showed a sensorimotor demyelinating neuropathy in 1 patient and were normal in another. Dysmorphic features included microcephaly, dolichocephaly, and low-set ears. Swallowing difficulties required percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy in patients from 2 families. Five patients died prematurely of aspiration pneumonia or uncontrolled seizures. The other 5 were aged 28, 23, 13, 10, and 3 years at their most recent evaluation (Mencacci et al., 2026).

paragraphs.text: In these patients, neuroimaging showed cerebral atrophy, loss of white matter, hypomyelination, small T2-hypointense thalami, a thin brainstem, and optic nerve atrophy. The corpus callosum was very thin, with a hypoplastic anterior commissure. Two patients also had mild cerebellar atrophy. In 1 patient the changes progressed rapidly between 9 months and 2 years of age. The 5 patients with homozygous splice-site variants also had developmental anomalies, such as dysgenesis of the corpus callosum and polymicrogyria (Mencacci et al., 2026).

paragraphs.text: Mencacci et al. (2026) also described 6 fetuses from 3 families with a distinct, severe prenatal phenotype that first came to attention because of reduced fetal movements. Intrauterine imaging in all 6 showed arthrogryposis multiplex congenita, hydrocephalus with aqueductal stenosis, agenesis of the corpus callosum, a markedly thin brainstem, cerebellar hypoplasia, and diffuse muscle atrophy. Growth parameters and other organ systems were normal, and the pregnancies were terminated between 21 and 25 weeks of gestation.

paragraphs.text: Brain histopathology in 2 of these fetuses showed microcephaly; hypoplasia of the thalamus, basal ganglia, and cerebellum; ventriculomegaly; aqueductal atresia; and absence of the corpus callosum. Major neuronal groups in the brainstem were hypoplastic, including the tegmental nuclei, inferior olivary nuclei, basis pontis, and dentate nucleus. There was widespread neuroaxonal degeneration, with axonal spheroids in the brainstem, cerebral hemispheres, and peripheral roots and nerves. The spheroids stained strongly for beta-amyloid precursor protein, neurofilament, and alpha-synuclein, consistent with neuroaxonal dystrophy. They did not stain for phosphorylated alpha-synuclein, tau, or TDP-43 (Mencacci et al., 2026).

paragraphs.text: Fisher et al. (2025) performed trio exome sequencing in 2 fetal sibs born to consanguineous Pakistani parents. Both fetuses were homozygous for a c.283C-T nonsense mutation in exon 3 of the BORCS5 gene, resulting in an arg95-to-ter (R95X) substitution, and each parent was heterozygous. One fetus was also homozygous for a missense variant of uncertain significance in the SCYL2 gene, for which the parents were heterozygous. Because the autopsy findings in the 2 sibs were identical, Fisher et al. (2025) raised the possibility that the SCYL2 variant did not contribute to the phenotype.

paragraphs.text: In 16 affected individuals from 9 unrelated families, Mencacci et al. (2026) identified 7 BORCS5 mutations, found by whole-exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing. In the index family, 2 affected sibs were compound heterozygous for a maternally inherited frameshift mutation (c.382_383delAG; L128Vfs*86) and a paternally inherited missense mutation (c.284G-A; R95Q). Their 2 unaffected older sibs were not carriers. All other affected individuals were homozygous. These mutations were R95Q in 2 sibs; a frameshift (c.316delG; A106Pfs*20) in 5 individuals from 2 unrelated Pakistani families; a splice-site mutation (c.202+1G-A) in 4 individuals from 2 unrelated families from Oman; and, in single individuals, a missense mutation (c.296A-C; H99P), a splice-site mutation (c.203-1G-T), and a nonsense mutation (c.417C-G; Y139X). Segregation analysis prioritized BORCS5 as the top candidate gene in each family. All of the variants were absent or exceedingly rare in gnomAD and other large databases. The 2 missense mutations affected fully conserved residues in a long alpha helix that, according to AlphaFold prediction, is likely essential for interaction with other BORC subunits. SpliceAI predicted that the 2 splice-site mutations would abolish the donor and acceptor splice sites of intron 2.

paragraphs.text: Mencacci et al. (2026) found that individuals homozygous for protein-truncating BORCS5 mutations, which cause complete loss of function, had a severe prenatally lethal phenotype. Features included arthrogryposis multiplex congenita, brain malformations, and neuroaxonal dystrophy. Individuals with missense mutations, either homozygous or compound heterozygous with a truncating mutation, had a chronic infantile-onset neurodegenerative course with progressive movement disorders and severe spasticity. Patients with homozygous splice-site mutations had a broadly similar presentation but more severe epilepsy and more pronounced neuroimaging abnormalities, particularly affecting the corpus callosum. Mencacci et al. (2026) considered this an intermediate phenotype between complete loss of function and missense mutations.

paragraphs.text: Mencacci et al. (2026) generated induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived forebrain neurons from 2 patients with R95Q/L128Vfs and an isogenic BORCS5-knockout line. Neurites of BORCS5-knockout neurons contained 60% fewer endolysosomes than control neurons, whereas the distribution of endolysosomes was unchanged in R95Q/L128Vfs neurons. In both the knockout and the patient neurons, LysoTracker-positive puncta were larger and more intense, and cathepsin B activity was reduced. Knockout neurons also had reduced lysosomal glucocerebrosidase activity. Their endolysosomal fractions contained less glucocerebrosidase and mature cathepsin B, and the cells accumulated autophagosomes, autolysosomes, and lysosomes. Mencacci et al. (2026) concluded that BORCS5 modulates lysosomal function as well as anterograde lysosomal transport. They proposed that this dual role may explain the different clinical phenotypes associated with different BORCS5 variants.

paragraphs.text: Mencacci et al. (2026) used CRISPR-Cas9 to knock out borcs5 in F0 zebrafish. At 3 days postfertilization, the knockout larvae had reduced body size, smaller eyes and heads, smaller brains, and fewer dopaminergic neurons. Later findings included enlarged ventricles, increased neuronal activation after exposure to pentylenetetrazole, reduced locomotor activity, shorter and less-branched motor axons, and disorganized muscle. Injection of wildtype human BORCS5 mRNA rescued these defects. When R95Q or H99P mRNA was expressed in borcs5-knockout embryos, the larvae had shorter bodies, smaller heads and eyes, and reduced swimming, although these defects were less severe than in knockout embryos.

allelic_variants.phenotype: Neurodegeneration, infantile-onset, with optic atrophy and structural brain abnormalities 2

paragraphs.text: In 5 individuals from 2 unrelated Pakistani families, Mencacci et al. (2026) identified a homozygous 1-bp deletion (c.316delG) in the BORCS5 gene, resulting in a frameshift (A106Pfs*20). The affected fetuses had arthrogryposis multiplex congenita, brain malformations, and neuroaxonal dystrophy, and the pregnancies were terminated. In transfected cells the mutant protein was truncated and expressed at lower levels, and it did not rescue perinuclear lysosomal clustering in BORCS5-knockout HeLa cells.

allelic_variants.phenotype: Neurodegeneration, infantile-onset, with optic atrophy and structural brain abnormalities 2

paragraphs.text: In a fetus of Arab descent with the severe prenatal form of NDOABA2, Mencacci et al. (2026) identified a homozygous c.417C-G transversion in the BORCS5 gene, resulting in a tyr139-to-ter (Y139X) substitution. Fibroblasts homozygous for Y139X had reduced BORCS5 mRNA, consistent with nonsense-mediated decay. They also had 93% less BORCS5 protein, reduced BORCS7 and SNAPIN, perinuclear clustering of lysosomes, multilamellar bodies, and reduced lysosomal proteolysis and glucocerebrosidase activity.
